_link.title: I can describe the potential applications of stem cells in regenerative medicine

toLevel2.question: What is one application of stem cells in regenerative medicine?

options.explanation: Epithelial stem cells can be used to grow new skin tissue for burns victims, which is a key application of regenerative medicine.
Antibiotics are produced by microorganisms or synthetically, not through stem cell therapy.
Stem cells are used for tissue regeneration, not energy generation.
While kidneys filter blood, stem cell therapy involves regenerating or replacing damaged tissues.

toLevel2.question: Which type of stem cell is used in leukaemia treatment?

options.explanation: Donor haematopoietic stem cells are transplanted into the patient's bone marrow to restore normal blood cell production.
Epithelial stem cells generate skin and lining tissues, not blood cells.
Neural stem cells differentiate into nerve cells, not blood cells needed for leukaemia treatment.
Muscle stem cells produce muscle tissue, not the blood cells required for leukaemia treatment.

toLevel2.question: How could stem cells potentially help patients with type 1 diabetes?

options.explanation: Stem cells could be used to generate new insulin-producing pancreatic cells to replace those destroyed in type 1 diabetes.
Stem cells themselves do not produce insulin; they would need to differentiate into functional pancreatic cells first.

options.text: By destroying the patient's immune system
options.explanation: The goal is to replace damaged cells, not destroy the immune system.

options.text: By filtering glucose from the blood
options.explanation: Stem cell therapy aims to restore insulin production, not filter glucose.

toLevel2.question: What is a potential advantage of growing organs from a patient's own stem cells?

options.explanation: Using a patient's own stem cells means the new organ has matching surface markers, so the immune system will not reject it.

options.text: It is cheaper than any other treatment
options.explanation: Cost is not the primary advantage discussed; avoiding immune rejection is the key benefit.

options.text: It works instantly without recovery time
options.explanation: Growing organs from stem cells still requires time and recovery; the advantage is reduced rejection risk.

options.text: It eliminates the need for surgery
options.explanation: Transplanting a grown organ would still require surgery; the advantage is compatibility.

toLevel2.question: What three broad categories of stem cell applications exist in regenerative medicine?

options.text: Tissue regeneration, cell deficiency treatment and organ transplants
options.explanation: These are the three main application areas: regenerating damaged tissue, replacing deficient cells, and potentially growing replacement organs.
These are different biotechnology applications, not the main categories of stem cell therapy.
These are conventional medical treatments, not stem cell application categories.
These relate to disease management, not regenerative medicine applications.

toLevel2.question: Haematopoietic stem cells can differentiate into red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
toLevel2.explanation: Haematopoietic stem cells are multipotent and can differentiate into all blood cell types including red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

toLevel2.question: Stem cells in regenerative medicine are only used for treating skin conditions.
toLevel2.explanation: Stem cells have multiple applications including treating leukaemia, type 1 diabetes, growing organs and tissue regeneration — not just skin conditions.

toLevel2.question: In leukaemia treatment, donor {{1}} stem cells are transplanted into the patient's {{2}} to restore blood production.
Stem cells can be used to grow skin for {{1}} victims using {{2}} stem cells.
Growing organs from a patient's own stem cells could avoid {{1}} by the immune system.

toLevel3.question: Why are haematopoietic stem cells described as multipotent in the context of leukaemia treatment?

options.text: Because they can differentiate into several blood cell types but not all body cell types
options.explanation: Multipotent means they can produce a range of related cell types (blood cells) but cannot become any cell type in the body like pluripotent cells can.

options.text: Because they can become any cell type in the body
options.explanation: That would describe pluripotent or totipotent cells, not multipotent cells.

options.text: Because they can only become one type of cell
options.explanation: That would describe unipotent cells. Haematopoietic stem cells can produce multiple blood cell types.

options.text: Because they divide faster than other stem cells
options.explanation: Potency refers to differentiation ability, not division speed.

toLevel3.question: Why is chemotherapy given before a bone marrow transplant in leukaemia treatment?

options.text: To destroy the cancerous bone marrow before new stem cells are introduced
options.explanation: Chemotherapy eliminates the diseased marrow, creating space for transplanted haematopoietic stem cells to establish healthy blood cell production.

options.text: To strengthen the patient's existing bone marrow
options.explanation: Chemotherapy destroys the existing marrow rather than strengthening it.

options.text: To help stem cells divide faster
options.explanation: Chemotherapy kills rapidly dividing cells; it does not promote stem cell division.

options.text: To prevent the stem cells from differentiating
options.explanation: The goal is for transplanted stem cells to differentiate into healthy blood cells.

toLevel3.question: Explain why using a patient's own stem cells for organ growth reduces the risk of rejection.

options.text: The cells share the patient's genetic identity, so the immune system recognises them as self
options.explanation: Organs grown from a patient's own stem cells have matching surface markers, so the immune system does not identify them as foreign.

options.text: The stem cells produce their own immune protection
options.explanation: Stem cells do not produce immune protection; compatibility depends on matching genetic markers.

options.text: The patient's immune system is disabled during the procedure
options.explanation: The advantage is genetic compatibility, not immune suppression.

options.text: Rejection only occurs with artificial organs, not biological ones
options.explanation: Rejection can occur with any transplanted tissue that the immune system identifies as foreign.

toLevel3.question: How does stem cell therapy for type 1 diabetes differ from insulin injections?

options.text: Stem cell therapy aims to permanently replace damaged cells, while injections only manage symptoms temporarily
options.explanation: Replacing faulty pancreatic cells with functional ones could restore natural insulin production, whereas injections must be administered regularly.

options.text: Insulin injections are more effective long-term
options.explanation: Injections manage symptoms but do not address the underlying cell deficiency; stem cell therapy aims for a permanent solution.

options.text: Stem cell therapy works instantly while injections take hours
options.explanation: Stem cell therapy requires time for differentiation and integration; the key difference is permanent vs temporary treatment.

options.text: There is no difference; both replace damaged cells
options.explanation: Insulin injections do not replace cells; they supply the hormone externally.

toLevel3.question: Why is tissue regeneration using stem cells particularly valuable for burns victims?

options.text: Because large areas of skin cannot regenerate naturally and need new tissue grown from stem cells
options.explanation: Severe burns destroy large areas of skin beyond the body's natural repair capacity, making stem cell-grown tissue essential for recovery.

options.text: Because burns only affect surface skin cells
options.explanation: Severe burns can affect multiple skin layers and underlying tissue, making regeneration critical.

options.text: Because skin cannot be transplanted from other donors
options.explanation: Skin grafts from donors are possible but carry rejection risks; stem cell-grown skin is genetically matched.

options.text: Because stem cells can prevent burns from occurring
options.explanation: Stem cells are used for treatment after burns, not for prevention.

toLevel3.question: What is the connection between stem cell potency and the range of medical applications?

options.text: Higher potency means a wider range of cell types can be generated for different treatments
options.explanation: Pluripotent cells can generate almost any cell type, offering broader therapeutic potential than multipotent or unipotent cells.

options.text: Lower potency cells are more useful in medicine
options.explanation: While specific potencies suit specific applications, higher potency generally offers more versatility.

options.text: Potency has no relationship to medical applications
options.explanation: The potency of a stem cell directly determines which cell types it can produce and therefore which conditions it can treat.

options.text: All stem cells have the same potency
options.explanation: Stem cells range from totipotent to unipotent, with different therapeutic capabilities.

toLevel3.question: Stem cell therapy for leukaemia works by directly killing cancer cells in the bone marrow.
toLevel3.explanation: Chemotherapy kills the cancerous cells. The stem cell transplant then replaces the destroyed marrow with healthy haematopoietic stem cells that produce normal blood cells.

toLevel3.question: Stem cell therapy for type 1 diabetes aims to {{1}} damaged pancreatic cells rather than just {{2}} symptoms with insulin injections.
Using a patient's own stem cells avoids rejection because the new tissue shares the patient's {{1}} identity.
In leukaemia treatment, {{1}} first destroys cancerous marrow before {{2}} stem cells are transplanted.

toLevel4.question: A patient with severe burns covering 40% of their body needs skin replacement. Which stem cell type and approach would be most appropriate?

options.text: Epithelial stem cells from the patient's own unburned skin to grow new tissue
options.explanation: Using the patient's own epithelial stem cells avoids rejection and can generate the skin tissue needed to cover the burned areas.

options.text: Haematopoietic stem cells from a donor
options.explanation: Haematopoietic stem cells produce blood cells, not skin tissue.

options.text: Neural stem cells from the patient's brain
options.explanation: Neural stem cells differentiate into nerve cells, not skin tissue.

options.text: Any stem cell type, as they all produce skin
options.explanation: Different stem cell types have different differentiation capabilities; epithelial stem cells are specific to skin and lining tissues.

toLevel4.question: A child with leukaemia undergoes a bone marrow transplant from a sibling donor. Predict what the transplanted cells will produce.

options.text: Red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
options.explanation: Haematopoietic stem cells in the transplanted marrow are multipotent and will differentiate into all major blood cell types.
Haematopoietic stem cells are multipotent and produce multiple blood cell types, not just red blood cells.
Haematopoietic stem cells differentiate into blood cells, not skin or muscle cells.
Haematopoietic stem cells produce blood cells specifically.

toLevel4.question: A researcher proposes growing a replacement kidney from a patient's induced pluripotent stem cells. What advantage does this have over using a donor kidney?

options.text: The patient's immune system would not reject the new kidney
options.explanation: Since induced pluripotent stem cells are derived from the patient's own cells, the grown kidney would be genetically matched, avoiding immune rejection.

options.text: The kidney would function better than a natural one
options.explanation: The advantage is compatibility, not necessarily superior function.

options.text: It would be ready for transplant immediately
options.explanation: Growing an organ from stem cells takes time; the advantage is immune compatibility.

options.text: It eliminates the need for any medical procedure
options.explanation: The organ would still need to be surgically transplanted.

toLevel4.question: A patient with type 1 diabetes receives stem cell-derived pancreatic cells. If the treatment is successful, what would you expect to observe?

options.text: The patient's blood sugar levels would regulate naturally without insulin injections
options.explanation: Functional stem cell-derived pancreatic cells would produce insulin, restoring natural blood sugar regulation.

options.text: The patient would need more insulin injections
options.explanation: Successful treatment would reduce or eliminate the need for external insulin.

options.text: The patient's bone marrow would improve
options.explanation: Pancreatic cell replacement targets insulin production, not bone marrow function.

options.text: The patient would develop immunity to diabetes
options.explanation: The treatment replaces damaged cells; it does not create immunity to the autoimmune process.

toLevel4.question: A bone marrow transplant patient develops an infection shortly after the procedure. Using your knowledge of the treatment process, explain why.

options.text: Chemotherapy destroyed their immune cells and the new stem cells have not yet produced enough white blood cells
options.explanation: Chemotherapy eliminates the patient's existing immune cells. The transplanted stem cells need time to differentiate into functional white blood cells.

options.text: The stem cells are causing the infection
options.explanation: Stem cells do not cause infections; the vulnerability comes from the destroyed immune system not yet being rebuilt.
Post-transplant infections are expected due to the temporary immune deficiency; they do not necessarily indicate failure.

options.text: Infections always occur after any medical procedure
options.explanation: The specific vulnerability here is due to the immune system being destroyed by chemotherapy before the transplant.

toLevel4.question: A scientist wants to treat a spinal cord injury using stem cells. Which potency level would be most suitable?

options.text: Pluripotent, because neural tissue requires multiple specialised cell types
options.explanation: Spinal cord repair requires various neural cell types. Pluripotent stem cells can differentiate into any cell type needed for the repair.

options.text: Unipotent, because only one cell type is needed
options.explanation: Spinal cord tissue contains multiple cell types, so unipotent cells would be too limited.

options.text: Totipotent, because they are the easiest to obtain
options.explanation: Totipotent cells are very difficult to obtain and ethically controversial; pluripotent cells are more practical.

options.text: Any potency would work equally well
options.explanation: The potency must match the range of cell types needed; lower potency may not produce all required types.

toLevel4.question: Two patients need stem cell treatment. Patient A receives cells from a matched donor. Patient B receives cells grown from their own tissue. Predict which patient has a higher risk of rejection.

options.text: Patient A, because donor cells may have different surface markers
options.explanation: Even matched donors may have some surface marker differences, creating a rejection risk. Patient B's own cells are a perfect genetic match.

options.text: Patient B, because self-derived cells are less stable
options.explanation: Self-derived cells are genetically identical to the patient and are not inherently less stable.
Patient A faces higher rejection risk because donor cells are not a perfect genetic match.
Patient A faces rejection risk from donor cell incompatibility.

toLevel4.question: After chemotherapy destroys cancerous marrow, transplanted stem cells need time to differentiate into {{1}}, leaving the patient temporarily vulnerable to {{2}}.
A kidney grown from a patient's own {{1}} stem cells would avoid {{2}} because the tissue is genetically matched.
Successful stem cell therapy for diabetes would restore natural {{1}} production, reducing the need for {{2}}.

toLevel5.question: Compare the use of haematopoietic stem cells in leukaemia treatment with the use of epithelial stem cells for burns treatment. What is the key similarity?

options.text: Both replace damaged or destroyed cells with functional ones derived from stem cells
options.explanation: In both cases, stem cells are used to regenerate cell populations that have been lost — blood cells in leukaemia and skin cells in burns.

options.text: Both use the same type of stem cell
options.explanation: Leukaemia uses haematopoietic stem cells while burns treatment uses epithelial stem cells — different types with different potencies.
Chemotherapy precedes bone marrow transplants but is not part of skin regeneration for burns.

options.text: Both treatments are fully established and routine
options.explanation: While bone marrow transplants are well established, some skin regeneration techniques are still developing.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why organ transplants using stem cells are still largely experimental despite the clear theoretical advantages.

options.text: Growing complex three-dimensional organs with correct structure and blood supply is technically very challenging
options.explanation: Organs require precise architecture, multiple cell types and functional blood vessel networks, which are extremely difficult to replicate from stem cells.

options.text: Because stem cells cannot form organ tissue
options.explanation: Stem cells can differentiate into organ tissue; the challenge is creating the complex structure of a complete organ.

options.text: Because patients always reject organs from stem cells
options.explanation: Using the patient's own stem cells should avoid rejection; the barrier is technical complexity.

options.text: Because there is no demand for organ transplants
options.explanation: There is significant demand and long waiting lists for organ transplants, making this research important.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate whether induced pluripotent stem cells could replace the need for embryonic stem cells in regenerative medicine.

options.text: They could largely replace embryonic cells since they offer similar potency without the ethical concerns of embryo destruction
options.explanation: iPSCs can be reprogrammed from adult cells to achieve pluripotency, avoiding embryo destruction while offering comparable differentiation potential.

options.text: They cannot replace embryonic cells because they have no potency
options.explanation: iPSCs are pluripotent and can differentiate into most cell types, similar to embryonic stem cells.

options.text: Embryonic stem cells are no longer used in research
options.explanation: Embryonic stem cells are still used in research, though iPSCs provide an alternative with fewer ethical issues.

options.text: iPSCs are identical to embryonic stem cells in every way
options.explanation: While similar in potency, iPSCs are derived differently and may have subtle differences in behaviour.

toLevel5.question: Analyse the potential risk if transplanted stem cells fail to differentiate correctly in a patient.

options.text: Undifferentiated stem cells could divide uncontrollably and form tumours
options.explanation: If stem cells do not differentiate as intended, their capacity for self-renewal could lead to uncontrolled proliferation, potentially forming tumours.

options.text: The cells would simply be absorbed by the body
options.explanation: Undifferentiated stem cells would not simply be absorbed; their continued division poses a tumour risk.

options.text: The patient would experience no effects
options.explanation: Incorrectly differentiating stem cells pose significant health risks including tumour formation.

options.text: The cells would revert to normal body cells
options.explanation: There is no mechanism for undifferentiated stem cells to automatically become appropriate body cells without proper signalling.

toLevel5.question: A researcher argues that multipotent stem cells are more suitable than pluripotent cells for certain treatments. Evaluate this claim.

options.text: This is valid because multipotent cells are already partially specialised, reducing tumour risk and directing differentiation more predictably
options.explanation: Multipotent cells have a more restricted differentiation pathway, making them safer and more predictable for specific tissue types.

options.text: This is incorrect because pluripotent cells are always better
options.explanation: Greater potency brings greater risk of incorrect differentiation and tumour formation; sometimes more restricted cells are preferable.

options.text: This is incorrect because multipotent cells cannot differentiate at all
options.explanation: Multipotent cells can differentiate into several related cell types within their lineage.

options.text: This is valid only if the patient is young
options.explanation: The suitability of multipotent cells depends on the treatment target, not the patient's age.

toLevel5.question: Compare the challenges of using stem cells for blood cell replacement versus whole organ replacement.

options.text: Blood cells are individual cells that self-organise, while organs require complex three-dimensional architecture
options.explanation: Blood cells function individually and can be produced by transplanted stem cells in bone marrow. Organs require precise spatial organisation of multiple cell types.

options.text: Blood cell replacement is more difficult than organ replacement
options.explanation: Blood cell replacement via bone marrow transplant is well established; organ replacement from stem cells remains experimental.
The structural complexity of organs presents far greater challenges than producing individual blood cells.
Both have challenges, but organ replacement presents substantially more complex ones.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why matching donor and recipient is important even when using adult stem cells for transplantation.

options.text: Mismatched surface markers would cause the recipient's immune system to attack the transplanted cells
options.explanation: The immune system identifies foreign cells by their surface markers. Mismatched donor cells trigger an immune response that destroys the transplant.

options.text: Matching is only important for organ transplants, not stem cells
options.explanation: Matching is important for any cell transplant to prevent immune rejection.

options.text: Unmatched cells would fail to divide
options.explanation: The cells could still divide, but the immune system would attack and destroy them.

options.text: Matching ensures the cells differentiate faster
options.explanation: Matching prevents rejection; it does not affect differentiation speed.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate the significance of stem cell research for the future of medicine.

options.text: It could transform treatment of degenerative diseases by enabling cell and tissue replacement rather than symptom management
options.explanation: Stem cell therapy offers the potential to cure conditions by replacing damaged cells and tissues, moving beyond merely managing symptoms.

options.text: It has no significant potential beyond current applications
options.explanation: Stem cell research continues to expand into new therapeutic areas with enormous potential.

options.text: It will replace all other forms of medicine
options.explanation: While transformative, stem cell therapy will complement rather than entirely replace existing medical approaches.

options.text: It is only relevant to cancer treatment
options.explanation: Stem cell applications extend to diabetes, burns, spinal injuries, organ failure and many other conditions.

toLevel5.question: If transplanted stem cells fail to differentiate correctly, they could divide {{1}} and potentially form {{2}}.
Blood cell replacement is more established than organ growth because blood cells function as {{1}} cells, while organs require complex {{2}} architecture.
